title: Why this practice
hookLine: the first rain on hot, dusty pavement, and a sutta that uses it to say what the unlovely is for
tomorrow: who would you want watching when nobody's watching?

lines: THE FIRST RAIN ON HOT PAVEMENT.
MEANT TO MAKE YOU HATE BODIES?
cards: The first rain after a long dry stretch has a smell: hot pavement, dust, something green. And the dust that was hanging in the air just settles.
A sutta uses that very moment to answer yesterday's question: is a practice like the unlovely meant to make you hate bodies? The answer comes out of a sad episode, told plainly in the text.

teach.b: The Buddha praises the foulness practice to his monks and goes on retreat alone. While he's away, some monks take it up with no balance. They come to loathe their own bodies, and some die by their own hand.
When he returns and sees fewer monks, he asks Ananda why, and then he gives them a different practice: the breath.

teach.h: THE BREATH, LIKE RAIN ON DUST.
teach.b: Peaceful, he calls it, and sublime, and he gives it an image: like a great rain late in the hot season that settles the swirling dust. Hold that picture.
A practice meant to cool craving had turned into a fire of its own, and the breath settled it.
Another sutta gives each practice its job. To a monk named Meghiya the Buddha says: the unlovely, to let go of lust. Goodwill, to let go of ill will.
The breath, to quiet busy thinking. Impermanence, to uproot the feeling I am. The unlovely sits right beside goodwill.

teach.h: AIMED AT CRAVING, NEVER AT PEOPLE.
teach.b: It's a cooling tool aimed at craving, never at people: not at someone else's body, and not at your own.
If thoughts of hating yourself or hurting yourself ever visit, you don't have to hold them alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help wherever you are.

how: Theravada teachers pair the foulness meditations with goodwill and mindfulness of breathing, and teach them as a remedy for craving under guidance, never as contempt for people; the episode in SN 54.9 is often cited as the reason for that care.

o: to frighten monks into keeping the rules out of fear
to prove the body is worthless and should be ignored
the reason behind it: to cool craving, never to hate

games.q: each practice and its job — tap the pairs.
p: to let go of ill will
to uproot the feeling I am

s: the foulness practice is meant to make you disgusted with people
it aims at craving. in the Buddha's words to Meghiya it sits right beside goodwill.
when some monks came to loathe their bodies, the Buddha taught them mindfulness of breathing
peaceful and sublime, he said, like a rain that settles the dust.
if a practice makes you feel worse about yourself, that means it's working
the texts record that turn as a harm, and the Buddha's answer was a gentler, settling practice.

games.q: a friend tried an online 'detox from looks' challenge and now calls her own body disgusting. what does the Buddha's response suggest?
o: keep going; feeling disgust means the challenge is working.
step back to something gentle and settling; the aim was cooling.
stop thinking about bodies at all, hers or anyone else's, ever.
games.why: when the unlovely turned into loathing, the Buddha gave the breath, like rain on dust. the aim was always to cool craving, never to hate.

practice: Rub your palms together until they're warm, and rest them over your eyes, or on the back of your neck, wherever feels tired. Let the breath settle, the way rain settles dust.
Before you lower your hands, thank this body, quietly, for carrying you through today.

wordCard.voice: Why this practice: the reason behind the unlovely. It's there to cool craving, side by side with goodwill, and never to turn into hate.

carryVoice: Your line: to cool, not to hate. The breath settles the dust. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 54.9 (Vesali Sutta: after the Buddha praises the foulness meditation and goes into seclusion, some monks become repelled by their bodies and take their lives; on his return he asks Ananda why the community has thinned, then teaches mindfulness of breathing as peaceful and sublime, which disperses unwholesome states as a great rain out of season settles the dust of the hot season)

Udana 4.1 / Anguttara Nikaya 9.3 (Meghiya Sutta: the unattractive to abandon lust, goodwill to abandon ill will, mindfulness of breathing to cut off thinking, perception of impermanence to uproot the conceit 'I am')
